issues.legal_issue: A later civil partition decree does not require income-tax authorities to recognize a partition that they previously rejected for tax purposes when the family was assessed as undivided and the tax-law appeal was not pursued by reference.
material_facts: A claim of partition under Section 25A was rejected, and the family was assessed as undivided.
A civil court passed a preliminary partition decree after the tax partition claim had been rejected.
The appeal against the tax decision was dismissed, and no reference challenging the Tribunal’s decision was sought.
issues.conclusion: The income-tax authorities were not bound by the later preliminary partition decree, and the family continued to be treated as undivided for purposes of the tax proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Section 25A(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1922 provided that a family assessed as undivided continued to be deemed an undivided Hindu family for purposes of the Act if no order accepting partition had been passed. The Court held that the later civil decree did not bind the income-tax authorities, particularly when no reference under the Act had been sought from the Tribunal’s decision. No earlier judicial case was cited for this holding.

rule.if: tax_partition_proceeding and partition_claim_rejected and family_assessed_as_undivided and later_civil_partition_decree and no_tax_reference_sought

predicates.tax_partition_proceeding: The matter concerns a tax proceeding in which a family’s claim that it had partitioned was considered.
predicates.partition_claim_rejected: The tax authority rejected the family’s claim that it had partitioned.
predicates.family_assessed_as_undivided: The family was assessed for tax as an undivided family.
predicates.later_civil_partition_decree: A civil court issued a partition decree after the tax authority had rejected the partition claim.
predicates.no_tax_reference_sought: The affected party did not seek a reference challenging the tax tribunal’s decision.

issues.definition: When a tax partition claim is rejected and the family is assessed as undivided, a later civil partition decree does not bind the tax authorities if no reference was sought from the tax tribunal’s decision.

issues.legal_issue: A junior member of an undivided Hindu family may manage the family as karta when the senior member gives up management and the other members consent.
material_facts: The senior family member had appointed a junior member to manage family affairs and had retired from active family management.
The junior member acted as karta, and the other family members did not dispute his authority.
The Court found that he had acted with the consent of the other members.
issues.conclusion: A junior member could act as karta with the consent of all the other members when the senior member gave up the right to manage.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the rule stated in Mulla’s Hindu Law, 14th edition, page 296: the senior member is ordinarily entitled to manage family property, but may give up that right, and a junior member may then be appointed manager. No judicial precedent was cited.

predicates.joint_family_management_dispute: The matter concerns who may manage the property and affairs of an undivided Hindu family.
predicates.senior_member_gave_up_management: The senior family member gave up the right to manage the family.
predicates.other_members_consented: The other family members consented to the junior member managing the family.

issues.definition: A junior member may manage an undivided Hindu family when the senior member gives up management and the other members consent.

issues.legal_issue: Tax assessment proceedings are not invalid as proceedings against a deceased person when notices are issued to the family under its business name, rather than to the deceased individual.
material_facts: The family’s business was carried on under the name of the deceased family head.
The notices were issued to the family under that name, not to the deceased individual.
The family’s managing member filed returns in response to the notices, and no objection that notices had been served on a deceased person was raised before the tax authorities.
issues.conclusion: The notices were not served on the deceased person, and the proceedings and assessments were not nullities on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the notices as having been issued to the family carrying on business under the assumed name, not to the deceased individual. It referred to notices under Sections 22 and 23 of the Income-tax Act, 1922, and Sections 142 and 143 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. No earlier judicial case was cited.

rule.if: tax_assessment_challenge and notices_addressed_to_family_business_name and notices_not_served_on_deceased_individual and family_manager_filed_returns

predicates.tax_assessment_challenge: The matter involves a challenge to tax assessment proceedings on the ground that notices were issued in the name of a deceased person.
predicates.notices_addressed_to_family_business_nam: The tax authority addressed notices to the family under the name used for its business.
predicates.notices_not_served_on_deceased_individua: The tax authority did not issue or serve the notices on the deceased individual personally.
predicates.family_manager_filed_returns: The family’s managing member filed returns in response to the notices.

issues.definition: When notices are addressed to a family under its business name and not served on a deceased individual, the assessments are not invalid as proceedings against that individual.

issues.legal_issue: A member’s share in family property and the income from that share may be reached to satisfy tax dues assessed against a family that continues to be treated as undivided for tax purposes.
material_facts: The family’s partition claim was rejected, and it continued to be treated as undivided for the tax proceedings.
The member challenged attachment of funds in a bank account operated by a receiver appointed in the partition suit.
The Court found that the member was bound by the assessments against the family and that his share in the family property or income from it was liable for the tax dues.
issues.conclusion: The member was bound by the family assessments, and his share in the family property or the income from it was liable for the tax dues.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 25A(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, the family continued to be deemed undivided for purposes of the Act because no order accepting partition had been passed. The Court accordingly held that the member was bound by the assessments and that his share or its income was liable for the family’s tax dues. No earlier judicial case was cited.

rule.if: tax_recovery_challenge and family_assessed_as_undivided and partition_claim_rejected and member_has_family_share_or_income

predicates.tax_recovery_challenge: The matter concerns a challenge to recovery of tax assessed against a family.
predicates.family_assessed_as_undivided: The family was assessed for tax as an undivided family.
predicates.partition_claim_rejected: The tax authority rejected the family’s claim that it had partitioned.
predicates.member_has_family_share_or_income: The member received or had a share in family property or income from that property.

issues.definition: A member’s share in family property or its income is answerable for family tax when the family was assessed as undivided and its partition claim was rejected.
